newsitem.title: USA: Call to ratify U.S.-Mexico maritime treaty revived.
newsitem.headline: Call to ratify U.S.-Mexico maritime treaty revived.

text.p: Huge oil finds in the deep waters of the Gulf of Mexico in recent years has revived calls for the Congress to ratify a two decade-old treaty which defines the maritime border between the United States and Mexico.
"It is one of (the State Dept's) high priorities," said a Washington official. "State has been consulting with industry and they seem poised to push for ratification."

Indeed, in a draft list of treaty priorities to be sent to by State to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee this week, the 1978 treaty is classed as a "high priority" for ratification, the second-highest priority category after "urgent."

The American Petroleum Institute (API), an industry group, is one of the chief proponents of ratification, reflecting oil company concerns about the security of potentially lucrative deep-water leases.
"We support the ratification of the treaty by the U.S. Senate. The API is making known its position on this issue to the State Department and U.S. Senate leaders," API spokesman Chris Kelley said.

The treaty was signed in Mexico City 19 years ago and was ratified by the Mexican Congress. The U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee passed it two years later but it was never put to a full vote and fell by the wayside until the recent surge in exploration interest.
"Only because technology has moved people further into the Gulf of Mexico did someone say 'this treaty isn't ratified'," says Genevieve Murphy, exploration affairs coordinator for the API.
In Mexico, the U.S. Congress' neglect to ratify the treaty has played into nationalist suspicions.

"U.S. Steals Our Oil," screamed local tabloids last month, responding to a campaign led by opposition Senator Jose Angel Conchello. Conchello has accused U.S. drilling firms of sucking up Mexican crude through horizontal drilling in a scheme he calls "Operation Drinking Straw."
Mexico's Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles has pledged to bring the issue before the U.S. government.
Reyes and U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena privately discussed the treaty at Binational Commission meetings on May 5, sources said.
A Foreign Ministry spokeswoman who declined to be named says the government is looking to resume bilateral discussions on the treaty next week.

While Reyes and state oil company Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) Chairman Adrian Lajous have denied that U.S. companies are drilling for oil on Mexican territory, the Mexican government has formed a commission comprised of representatives of Pemex and the ministries of foreign affairs and energy to check into the accusations.

Any suggestion of U.S. impingement on Mexican territory or in the nation's coveted oil reserves traditionally sparks local outrage, evoking memories of Mexico's nationalization of its hydrocarbon reserves in 1938.
"It is a delicate topic that gets to all Mexicans very deeply and we are paying close attention to it," Reyes has said.
